name: Convoy of Hope (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build, by each branch's share of the modelled outcome: the US 4.9% (partner resourcing's US goods, US disaster relief, community events and rural initiatives); the rest (children's feeding, agriculture, women's programmes, goods and medicines sent abroad, and the disasters abroad, most of them unnamed and in or near the programme countries) split equally over 15 programme countries named in Convoy's 2024 annual report or known feeding countries (a judgment: no country split is published).
summary: Convoy of Hope, a faith-based charity in Springfield, Missouri, passed $532 million of donated food, clothing, household goods and medicines (at the donors' wholesale values) to partners in the US and abroad in 2024 and spent $123 million of its own ($66 million on its four programmes, the rest on fundraising and management; audited accounts): partner resourcing, community development (a school-day meal for 635,000 children abroad, and training for 39,000 farmers and 61,000 women and girls), community events in US cities, and relief in 53 US and 46 overseas disasters. The result, about 0.06 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, comes mostly from the school meals, valued as food for very poor children, then the farmers' and women's training and the goods and medicines sent abroad; goods handed out in the US add little on the site's log-income scale, and Convoy is credited only with its own spending's share of the resources behind the donated goods. Every branch rests on Convoy's own counts and judged prices and splits, and every branch is discounted for missing data; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, how poor the children fed are, and what the donated goods' recorded values are worth to the people who get them.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Partner resourcing: people served (the rest of Convoy's count)
rows.formula: people_served_total - dus_people - dint_people - feed_children - ag_participants - wom_participants - rur_people - ev_guests
rows.explainer: Convoy publishes no count for partner resourcing; its total less the other programmes' counts, about 40 million, is the people partners served with its goods. The goods' value enters almost in proportion (each person gets a few dollars, a small share of consumption), so this count barely moves the result.

rows.label: People reached by the disaster responses abroad (the crisis branch)
rows.explainer: The template's crisis rows (mortality, months exposed, consumption) describe the international disaster responses, so its people reached are that branch's 3.0 million; the other branches count their own people below.

rows.label: Cost per person served, all programmes
rows.explainer: Convoy's own spending, overhead included, over everyone it counts as served: context only, since most of them got a small share of donated goods through partners.

rows.label: Dominican Republic: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.label: Philippines: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.label: Programme countries abroad: survey consumption per person (stand-in mean)
rows.formula: avg(cons_dom, cons_hnd, cons_ken, cons_mwi, cons_npl, cons_phl)
rows.explainer: Convoy works in 65 countries; its feeding and community-development countries span Central America and the Caribbean (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Haiti, the Dominican Republic), East and Southern Africa (Ethiopia, Tanzania, Kenya, Malawi), West Africa (Burkina Faso, Niger), Asia (Nepal, the Philippines) and Moldova. Stand-in: the equal mean of the six such countries with a full set of survey figures on the site (survey mean, growth since the survey, price level); Guatemala and El Salvador have survey means but no price level or growth there, and Convoy publishes no split of children by country.

rows.label: Consumption of the people served abroad, as a share of the stand-in mean
rows.explainer: Convoy targets poor communities (schoolchildren in villages where families can prepare one or two simple meals a day, smallholders, marginalised women); the poorest fifth in these surveys consume about 40% of the mean. Judgment 60% (40-90%), as Samaritan's Purse's shoebox recipients.

rows.label: Consumption per person of the people served abroad, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The stand-in mean times the recipients' share: the base against which the goods are valued on the log scale.

rows.label: Price level of the programme countries against the US (market prices)
rows.explainer: The World Bank's ratio of each country's consumption prices to US prices, the same six countries: food and goods cost about a third as much at local market prices as in the US.

rows.label: Consumption per person of low-income Americans served with food and goods, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The shared US figures the site's food-bank and goods models read: consumer spending per person times food-aid recipients' share of it.

rows.label: Donated food: US retail value per dollar of its recorded wholesale value
rows.explainer: Convoy books donated food at the donors' wholesale fair value checked against a third-party website (note B); a household getting it saves what it would pay at retail. 1.25 (1.1-1.5), as Feeding America's model's retail-to-wholesale ratio for donated food.

rows.label: Donated clothing, household goods and supplies: US value per dollar of their recorded value
rows.explainer: Corporate surplus clothing and household goods are booked at the donors' wholesale valuations, which can overstate what slow-moving stock would sell for. 0.85 (0.5-1.1); with the in-kind step below it gives 60% of the recorded value, World Vision US's domestic model's figure for the same kind of goods.

rows.label: Programme countries: food prices against all consumption prices (both relative to the US)
rows.explainer: Food is traded, so in poorer countries its price level is closer to the US one than the overall consumption level, which cheap local services pull down (the Balassa-Samuelson pattern in the World Bank's International Comparison Program, where food and non-alcoholic beverages typically stand at about half to two thirds of US prices in low- and lower-middle-income countries against about a third to two fifths for all household consumption). The site has no food price-level fact; judgment 1.4 (1.1-1.9).

rows.label: Donated food sent abroad: local value per dollar of its recorded value
rows.explainer: Valued at local market prices, not US ones (families/humanitarian-relief.md): the US retail value times the programme countries' price level for food.

rows.label: Donated goods sent abroad: local value per dollar of their recorded value
rows.explainer: The same step for clothing, household goods and supplies sent abroad: what they would cost in local markets.

rows.label: Food given in kind: worth to the household per dollar of its value
rows.explainer: Families can't choose what they get; staple food is mostly infra-marginal (they would have bought as much), so it is worth close to its price. 80% (60-95%), as Feeding America's model's in-kind cash equivalence for food.

rows.label: Goods given in kind: worth to the household per dollar of their value
rows.explainer: Clothing, shoes, hygiene and household goods are further from what families would have bought than food, and some go unused (TOMS shoes in El Salvador: most children already had a pair, Wydick et al. 2018). 70% (45-90%); with the price step above, 60% of recorded value, as World Vision US's domestic goods.

rows.label: Partner resourcing: share of the donated goods sent abroad
rows.explainer: Convoy supplies 'like-minded organizations throughout the world' (note A) from its Springfield distribution centre; most of its partners are US churches, pantries and nonprofits, and 57% of the goods ($297 million of $532 million) went straight from the donor to partners (note J), typically US shipments of surplus stock. No split is published: judgment 30% (15-55%).

rows.label: Partner resourcing: food's share of the donated goods
rows.explainer: Of the goods donated in 2024, food was 48% ($259 million), clothing and household goods 37% ($203 million), medicines and medical supplies 13% ($70 million), disaster supplies 1% (note J); the feeding programme and disaster response take a larger share of the food. Judgment 40% (30-50%).

rows.label: Partner resourcing: medicines' and medical supplies' share of the donated goods
rows.explainer: Medicines and medical supplies were 13% of the goods donated in 2024 ($69.8 million, up from $43.4 million in 2023, note J), mostly passed to partners. Judgment 15% (8-22%).

rows.label: Partner resourcing: clothing and household goods' share
rows.explainer: The rest of the goods: clothing, household goods, hygiene and other supplies.

rows.label: Partner resourcing in the US: goods' worth to the households
rows.formula: pr_gik * (1 - pr_abroad_share) * (pr_food_share * food_us_price_ratio * food_equivalence + (pr_nonfood_share + pr_med_share) * nonfood_us_price_ratio * nonfood_equivalence)
rows.explainer: Goods kept in the US, at US prices and their in-kind worth; medical supplies in the US are valued like other goods (what the clinic or family saves), since their health value at US prices is mostly cost saved.

rows.label: Partner resourcing abroad: food and goods' worth to the households
rows.formula: pr_gik * pr_abroad_share * (pr_food_share * food_abroad_price_ratio * food_equivalence + pr_nonfood_share * nonfood_abroad_price_ratio * nonfood_equivalence)
rows.explainer: Food and goods sent abroad, at local prices and their in-kind worth; medicines abroad are valued as health below, not here.

rows.label: Partner resourcing in the US: people served
rows.explainer: Partner resourcing's people split as its goods are.

rows.label: Partner resourcing abroad: people served
rows.explainer: Partner resourcing's people split as its goods are.

rows.label: Partner resourcing in the US: log-consumption gain per person
rows.explainer: A year's goods against a year's consumption of the low-income Americans served.

rows.label: Partner resourcing abroad: log-consumption gain per person
rows.explainer: A year's goods against a year's consumption of the people served abroad.

rows.label: Medicines sent abroad: local value per dollar of their recorded value
rows.explainer: Convoy books donated medicines at the donors' 'wholesale acquisition cost' or 'average wholesale price' (note B), US list prices; the same products cost a fraction of that in poorer countries' tenders and generic markets. 0.3 (0.12-0.6), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: Medicines and medical supplies sent abroad, at local prices
rows.explainer: The partner-resourcing medicines sent abroad, at what the recipient health facilities would pay locally.

rows.label: GDP per person where the medicines go, US$
rows.explainer: Partner clinics and missions in Convoy's programme countries (Central America and the Caribbean, Africa, Asia). 2,000 dollars (1,200-4,000), as Direct Relief's model for its recipients outside Ukraine.

rows.label: Health systems' cost per healthy year at the margin, as a share of GDP per person
rows.explainer: What the recipient health systems' next dollar buys (the supply-side threshold): Woods et al. (2016, Value in Health) estimate 11-51% of GDP per person for El Salvador and 1-51% for Malawi; Ochalek et al. (2018) find few low- and middle-income countries above 1x GDP per person. 30% (12-60%), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: Cost of a healthy year at the margin in the recipient health systems
rows.explainer: GDP per person times the share: the health a dollar of medicines frees or buys.

rows.label: Health per dollar of the donated medicines against the health system's marginal dollar
rows.explainer: Direct Relief's model takes 1 (0.5-2.5) for medicines its partners request through an ordering system; Convoy passes medical stock to partner clinics and missions with less matching to requests, more often surplus and short-dated. 0.7 (0.3-2).

rows.label: Medicines abroad: healthy years before adjustments
rows.explainer: The medicines' local value over the cost of a healthy year at the margin, times their usefulness.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: illness part (years lived with disability averted)
rows.explainer: The share of the healthy years that is illness, the site's figure for medicines in low- and middle-income countries; the rest is deaths, valued by age below.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: deaths averted
rows.explainer: The death part of the healthy years, in deaths, by the site's deaths per DALY for medicines in low- and middle-income countries, so each is valued at the shared value of a death.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: share of deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: Mixed primary care (antibiotics, chronic-disease drugs, supplies) for all ages. 25% (10-40%), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: of deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: Few deaths in this age band in mixed primary care. 5% (2-12%), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: of deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: Most adult deaths averted by drugs are of older adults (chronic disease). 30% (15-45%), as Direct Relief's model; the rest valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Disaster response: share of spending and goods in the US
rows.explainer: 2024 had large US responses (Hurricanes Helene and Milton: 112 communities in six states, more than 6 million pounds to 325,000 people; 14.0 million pounds in all US responses) and 46 smaller responses abroad with 27.3 million meals (Hope Quarterly 37, pp. 12 and 17). No split is published: judgment 55% (40-70%).

rows.label: Disaster response grants: share that buys food and relief goods

rows.explainer: Convoy's responses send truckloads of food, water, hygiene kits, totes, tarps, air purifiers and cleanup kits (Hope Quarterly 37, pp. 4 and 16); disaster supplies were $6.5 million of the goods donated (note J), the food and water much more. Judgment 65% (45-80%).

rows.label: US disasters: goods' worth to the households
rows.formula: dr_us_share * (dr_gik * (dis_food_share * food_us_price_ratio * food_equivalence + (1 - dis_food_share) * nonfood_us_price_ratio * nonfood_equivalence) + (dr_relief_purchases + dr_grants * dr_grants_relief_share) * food_equivalence)
rows.explainer: The US share of the donated relief goods at US prices and their in-kind worth, plus the relief bought by Convoy and by partners with its grants, at cost.

rows.label: US disasters: time over which the goods are used (years)
rows.explainer: Food, water and hygiene supplies handed out in the weeks after a hurricane or tornado, used up within about a month. 0.08 years (0.03-0.25).

rows.label: US: consumption per person of the poorest fifth, as a share of the mean
rows.explainer: The Consumer Expenditure Survey's lowest quintile, per person, from the shared US figures, as Team Rubicon's model reads them.

rows.label: US disasters: survivors' consumption against the poorest fifth's
rows.explainer: People who line up for relief supplies after a hurricane are mostly lower-income households in the hit communities, a little better off than the poorest fifth. 1.2 (0.9-1.6), as Team Rubicon's model for disaster survivors.

rows.label: US disasters: consumption per person of the people served, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The base against which the relief goods are valued.

rows.label: US disasters: log-consumption gain per person
rows.explainer: Goods used up over t years raise consumption only in those months: t × ln(1 + v ÷ (b × t)) (families/humanitarian-relief.md).

rows.label: Disasters abroad: goods' worth per person served
rows.formula: (1 - dr_us_share) * (dr_gik * (dis_food_share * food_abroad_price_ratio * food_equivalence + (1 - dis_food_share) * nonfood_abroad_price_ratio * nonfood_equivalence) + (dr_relief_purchases + dr_grants * dr_grants_relief_share) * food_equivalence) / dint_people
rows.explainer: The share of the relief goods abroad at local prices and their in-kind worth, plus the relief bought by Convoy and its partners at cost, per person served: a few dollars each.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: meals a person eats a day
rows.explainer: The people fed in a response eat two to three meals a day; Convoy's meals are part of that. 2.5 (2-3).

rows.label: Disasters abroad: time the food covers (years)
rows.explainer: Meals per person over meals a day: about four days of food per person served, the window over which the goods raise consumption and over which excess deaths can be averted.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: survivors' consumption against the programme countries' stand-in mean
rows.explainer: Convoy names few of its 46 responses abroad (Brazil, Spain and Chile together under 1% of the meals); most are in or near its programme countries, where survivors had lost homes and income for a time. 1 (0.6-2) times the programme countries' mean.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: consumption per person of the people served, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The stand-in mean times the ratio.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: log-consumption gain per person
rows.explainer: t × ln(1 + v ÷ (b × t)) over the days the food covers (families/humanitarian-relief.md).

rows.label: Disasters abroad: normal death rate of the people served (per person-year)
rows.explainer: Stand-in: the crude death rates of two of Convoy's programme countries the site has (UN WPP), about 7 per 1,000 a year.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: death rate in the weeks after the disaster, without the response
rows.explainer: Sudden floods, fires and storms kill mostly on impact; in the weeks after, death rates rise a little (disrupted water, care and food), far below the 1 per 10,000 a day (0.037 a year) emergency threshold of famine settings. Judgment 0.009 (0.007-0.015), about 30% above normal.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: share of the excess deaths the food and goods avert
rows.explainer: Food and water in a sudden-onset disaster outside famine settings avert little of the excess, which comes from injury, disease and lost care. 5% (0-15%), as World Central Kitchen's model for poorer countries' crises.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: deaths averted per person served
rows.explainer: Excess deaths only, over the days the response covers.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: share of the deaths averted under five
rows.explainer: A stand-in: the site's WHO Global Health Estimates split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa, as Samaritan's Purse's model, for the infection deaths a crisis worsens.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split, as Samaritan's Purse's model.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split; the rest valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: illness averted per person (healthy years)
rows.explainer: Not counted separately: the food and goods are valued as consumption and the deaths as deaths; illness averted by a few days' food is small and sits in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Community development: food and outreach bought, 2024

source.title: Convoy of Hope, consolidated financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023 (Batts Morrison Wales & Lee, P.A., report dated June 10, 2025): Convoy-of-Hope-Financial-Statements-BMWL-2023-2024.pdf on convoyofhope.org
source.page: p. 14 (note K, functional allocation of expenses, 2024)

rows.explainer: Cash community development spent on food and outreach (the line's second column), mostly local food for the feeding programme: valued at cost.

rows.label: Community development: grants to partner ministries, 2024

source.title: Convoy of Hope, consolidated financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2023 (Batts Morrison Wales & Lee, P.A., report dated June 10, 2025): Convoy-of-Hope-Financial-Statements-BMWL-2023-2024.pdf on convoyofhope.org
source.page: p. 14 (note K, functional allocation of expenses, 2024)

rows.explainer: Cash community development granted to the local churches and partners that run the feeding, agriculture and women's programmes (the line's second column).

rows.label: Community development grants: share that buys food for the meals
rows.explainer: Local churches and partners cook and serve the meals (Hope Quarterly 37, p. 18); part of the grants buys local food, the rest pays cooks, kitchens and the other programmes. Judgment 40% (10-80%).

rows.label: Community development: share of its donated goods that is food for the children's meals
rows.explainer: Community development's $84.4 million of donated goods is mostly food shipped to the feeding programme's countries (Convoy plans its own meal factory for the programme, Hope Quarterly 37, p. 5); the rest is supplies for agriculture, women's groups and rural initiatives. Judgment 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Children's feeding: the meals' worth to the children
rows.formula: (cd_gik * feed_gik_share * food_abroad_price_ratio + cd_food_purchases + cd_grants * cd_grants_food_share) * food_equivalence
rows.explainer: Donated food at local prices plus the food bought locally, by Convoy and by its partners with its grants, times its in-kind worth.

rows.label: Children's feeding: log-consumption gain per child
rows.explainer: A school year's meals against the child's share of household consumption; the meal frees what the family would have fed the child, so it counts as consumption, valued for the child alone (slightly below spreading it over the household).

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: consumption gain per household member
rows.explainer: Training-only livelihood programmes (farmer field schools, business and savings training) raise consumption little on average in trials; Convoy's greenhouse farmers' tripled tomato incomes are a case, not the average. 1.5% (0-5%), as World Vision's livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Gains from training fade as practices lapse or spread to neighbours. 2 years (1-4), as World Vision's livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: share of the year's participants who are new
rows.explainer: The counts are each year's participants in programmes that run several years (the featured farmer in Nepal joined four years before, Hope Quarterly 37, p. 19), so a participant appears in several yearly counts. New participants get the whole gain over the years it lasts; those continuing get one more year of it. Judgment 50% (30-80%).

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: household size
rows.explainer: The participant's household shares the gain: the site's household sizes for four programme regions.

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: log-consumption gain per household member
rows.explainer: For new participants the yearly gain over the years it lasts, discounted; for continuing ones (Convention 3, flows not stocks) the one more year this year's spending adds.

rows.label: Deaths averted by higher consumption, as a share of its value (poor households abroad)
rows.explainer: More food and income in very poor households lowers child mortality a little (cash transfers in Kenya and elsewhere reduce infant deaths); the site's models of livelihoods and cash abroad add these deaths as a share of the consumption gain's value, moving with the value of a life. 20% (0-50%), as World Vision's livelihoods branch; applied to the school meals, the training and the goods sent abroad, not to a few days of disaster food.

rows.label: Women's and girls' programmes: gain against the agriculture programme's
rows.explainer: Women's and girls' empowerment mixes small-business and savings training with life skills; many participants are girls still in school, whose income gain comes later. 0.7 (0.3-1.2).

rows.label: Rural initiatives (US): goods' worth to the households
rows.explainer: The pounds delivered at the shared wholesale value of a pound of donated food (Feeding America's fiscal year to June 2025, half of it in 2024; its 2024 figure was 1.97 dollars), at retail and in-kind worth (most of the resources are food).

rows.label: Rural initiatives (US): log-consumption gain per person
rows.explainer: A year's goods against a year's consumption of the low-income Americans served.

rows.label: Community events: food's share of the donated goods
rows.explainer: Events hand out groceries (287,000+ bags), children's shoes (17,000+ pairs), clothing and household goods, and supply the 3,393 organisations and churches taking part (Hope Quarterly 37, p. 21). Judgment 40% (25-60%).

rows.label: Community events: goods' worth to the households
rows.formula: ev_gik * (ev_food_share * food_us_price_ratio * food_equivalence + (1 - ev_food_share) * nonfood_us_price_ratio * nonfood_equivalence)
rows.explainer: The events' donated goods at US prices and their in-kind worth; the screenings, haircuts and job help are in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Community events: log-consumption gain per guest
rows.explainer: The goods per guest against a year's consumption of low-income Americans; goods passed on to partners' clients reach more people, which on this nearly linear scale changes little.

rows.label: Donated goods: share that wouldn't have reached similar people anyway
rows.explainer: Corporate donors give surplus to many channels (Feeding America's food banks, Good360, World Vision, other charities) or liquidate it; without Convoy much would reach similar people another way. 60% (35-85%), between Feeding America's model's 50% for donated food and World Vision US's 67% for donated goods. Also used for the events' and rural goods.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: share that wouldn't have reached the patients anyway
rows.explainer: Other channels (Direct Relief, Americares, MAP International) ship donated medicines to similar clinics. 75% (50-90%), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: Medicines abroad: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The health value comes from the health system's marginal cost per healthy year, not a trial of these medicines; that uncertainty is in the usefulness row. 1 (0.8-1.1), as Direct Relief's model.

rows.label: US disasters: share that wouldn't have been delivered anyway
rows.explainer: US disasters draw FEMA, the Red Cross, food banks and many church groups; Convoy's trucks often arrive first, but much of the same food and water would have come. 55% (30-80%), as Team Rubicon's model.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: share other responders wouldn't have delivered
rows.explainer: Most responses abroad are in Convoy's poorer programme countries, where government relief is thin and appeals underfunded, and local churches and other agencies also respond. 70% (45-90%), as Samaritan's Purse's relief abroad.

rows.label: Disasters abroad: evidence adjustment for the deaths averted
rows.explainer: The deaths averted rest on judged rates, not a mortality survey of the people served. 85% (70-100%), as Samaritan's Purse's relief abroad; the goods, valued at their worth, take no evidence step.

rows.label: Children's feeding: share of the meals the children wouldn't have had anyway
rows.explainer: Some programme countries run national school-meal programmes (Kenya, Ethiopia, Guatemala) that could reach some of the same schools; Convoy's schools are mostly ones without. 85% (60-95%).

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The gain is a judgment from the literature on similar training, not a trial of Convoy's programmes. 80% (50-100%), as World Vision's livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: share of the gain that wouldn't have come anyway
rows.explainer: Few other programmes train the same farmers and women; some would have improved anyway, which the gain's judgment against no programme already nets out. 90% (70-100%), as World Vision's livelihoods branch.

rows.label: Partners' and volunteers' resources, as a share of Convoy's and the donors'
rows.explainer: Partner churches, pantries and nonprofits store and hand out the goods, and volunteers sort and serve (7,000+ at the Springfield headquarters, 800+ on field teams, local churches at every event and response; Hope Quarterly 37, pp. 13 and 21). Feeding America's model puts the network's handing-out cost near 0.25 dollars a pound, about 13% of a pound's 1.90-dollar value. 15% (5-35%).

rows.label: Partner resourcing: donated goods at local value (the donors' resources)
rows.formula: pr_gik * ((1 - pr_abroad_share) * (pr_food_share * food_us_price_ratio + (pr_nonfood_share + pr_med_share) * nonfood_us_price_ratio) + pr_abroad_share * (pr_food_share * food_abroad_price_ratio + pr_nonfood_share * nonfood_abroad_price_ratio + pr_med_share * med_abroad_price_ratio))
rows.explainer: The donors' goods valued at local prices, as in the value rows (before the in-kind step, which is about worth to the family, not what was given).

rows.label: Partner resourcing: Convoy's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Convention 2: Convoy's own spending on the line, with overhead, over that plus the donors' goods at local value plus partners' and volunteers' resources.

rows.label: Community development: the feeding programme's share of the line's own spending
rows.explainer: No split is published. Freight ($4.1 million) and the bought food go mostly with the meals, the travel ($2.8 million) mostly with the field teams and training, staff and grants to both (note K). Judgment 50% (35-70%).

rows.label: Children's feeding: Convoy's share of the resources
rows.formula: cd_cash * feed_cash_share * overhead_ratio / ((cd_cash * feed_cash_share * overhead_ratio + cd_gik * feed_gik_share * food_abroad_price_ratio) * (1 + partner_resources_share))
rows.explainer: Convention 2, as above: the feeding programme's share of the line's own spending, with overhead, over that plus the donated food at local prices plus the partners' and volunteers' resources (local churches cook and serve the meals).

rows.label: Training and rural initiatives: Convoy's share of the resources
rows.formula: cd_cash * (1 - feed_cash_share) * overhead_ratio / ((cd_cash * (1 - feed_cash_share) * overhead_ratio + cd_gik * (1 - feed_gik_share) * food_us_price_ratio) * (1 + partner_resources_share))
rows.explainer: Convention 2 for the rest of community development: its own spending over that plus its donated goods (mostly the rural initiatives' food, at US prices) plus partners' and volunteers' resources.

rows.label: Community events: donated goods at local value
rows.explainer: The events' goods at US prices.

rows.label: Community events: Convoy's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Convention 2, as above: the events are run with volunteers from local churches, businesses and civic groups.

rows.label: Disaster response: donated goods at local value
rows.formula: dr_gik * (dr_us_share * (dis_food_share * food_us_price_ratio + (1 - dis_food_share) * nonfood_us_price_ratio) + (1 - dr_us_share) * (dis_food_share * food_abroad_price_ratio + (1 - dis_food_share) * nonfood_abroad_price_ratio))
rows.explainer: The relief goods at US prices for the US share and local prices abroad.

rows.label: Disaster response: Convoy's share of the resources
rows.explainer: Convention 2, as above: local volunteers, churches, police and businesses help hand out the supplies (Hope Quarterly 37, p. 12).

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Every count here is Convoy's own and unaudited (the auditor gives no assurance on the impact summary): goods unused or resold by partners, spoilage, people counted at several distributions. 85% (70-95%) for every branch, as Samaritan's Purse's and World Vision's models.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Up to 20% of restricted gifts may go to overhead and the board may move restricted money to other projects (Hope Quarterly 37, p. 15), so restricted giving is fungible; no matching funds. 1 (0.9-1.05).

rows.explainer: Purchased supplies and donated goods in the warehouses at year end (note G).

rows.label: pr: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for partner resourcing's goods (US and abroad): people are Convoy's total less the other counts and the goods' worth judged prices, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: med: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for the medicines abroad: the medicines' health is their local value over a judged marginal cost per healthy year, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: dr: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for disaster response (US and abroad): the split, prices and death rates are judgments over Convoy's own counts, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: feed: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for children's feeding: the meals' value is judged from spending and Convoy's own count of children, with no measured nutrition or schooling outcome, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: liv: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for agriculture and women's programmes: the gain is a judgment from other programmes' trials, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: rur: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for rural initiatives: the goods' value is judged from pounds, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: ev: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin (templates.md Convention 12) for community events: the goods' worth is judged and the guests are Convoy's own count, so the branch reads the shared missing-data slider.

rows.label: Partner resourcing goods: all adjustments
rows.formula: pr_counterfactual_adj * pr_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * pr_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Goods valued at their worth take no evidence step (families/humanitarian-relief.md).

rows.label: Medicines abroad: all adjustments
rows.formula: med_evidence_adj * med_counterfactual_adj * pr_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * med_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: The medicines share partner resourcing's credit share.

rows.label: US disasters: all adjustments
rows.formula: dus_counterfactual_adj * dr_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * dr_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Goods at their worth: no evidence step.

rows.label: Disasters abroad, goods: all adjustments
rows.formula: dint_counterfactual_adj * dr_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * dr_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Goods at their worth: no evidence step.

rows.label: Disasters abroad, deaths averted: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The goods' adjustments times the evidence step for the deaths.

rows.label: Children's feeding: all adjustments
rows.formula: feed_counterfactual_adj * feed_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * feed_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Food at its worth: no evidence step.

rows.label: Agriculture and women's programmes: all adjustments
rows.formula: liv_evidence_adj * liv_counterfactual_adj * cdo_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * liv_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Each step for the training programmes.

rows.label: Rural initiatives: all adjustments
rows.formula: pr_counterfactual_adj * cdo_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * rur_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Donated goods' counterfactual, the rest of community development's credit share.

rows.label: Community events: all adjustments
rows.formula: pr_counterfactual_adj * ev_attribution_share * implementation_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * ev_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Donated goods' counterfactual, the events' credit share.

rows.label: Unmodelled: schooling and nutrition from the school meals
rows.explainer: School meals raise enrolment and attendance and, less surely, learning and girls' schooling (Snilstveit et al. 2016, 3ie systematic review 24; Aurino et al. 2023 on Ghana's programme), beyond the food's value counted above. The feeding branch is about two thirds of the result; a tenth more there: +6.6% (0-20%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: screenings, haircuts and job help at the events
rows.explainer: Free medical and dental screenings, haircuts and job-placement help at the community events (note A); small next to the goods. +0.3% (0-1%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: wells and water filters
rows.explainer: Convoy digs wells for some villages in Africa and hands out water filters in floods (Hope Quarterly 37, p. 6); unsized. +0.5% (0-2%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: surplus kept out of landfill
rows.explainer: Donated surplus food and goods that would otherwise be dumped avoid landfill emissions; small at the site's value of a tonne of CO2e. +0.3% (0-1%).

rows.label: Unmodelled: free food and goods lowering local sellers' prices
rows.explainer: Free food and clothing can undercut local farmers, traders and tailors near distributions; Convoy's volumes per community are small. -1% (-3% to 0), as Samaritan's Purse's model.

rows.label: Unmodelled: aid tied to church outreach
rows.explainer: Convoy is faith-based and works through local churches; events connect guests to churches. Aid is not conditional on faith, but in some places this can deter people or strain relations with other faiths. -0.5% (-3% to 0), smaller than Samaritan's Purse's -1% because Convoy runs no evangelism programme.

rows.label: Effects not modelled (share of the modelled value)
rows.formula: ue_school_meals_share + ue_event_services_share + ue_wells_share + ue_landfill_share + ue_food_aid_market_share + ue_proselytism_share
rows.explainer: The side effects above, each with its sign.
